F01.determination: Freight must not be added as a separate contributing interest: the bill terms make it fully earned and non-returnable, so it is included in the USD 367,418,702 cargo value.

F02.determination: The equipment population avoids double counting: two shipper-owned containers sit in cargo, while the separate USD 14,315,119 equipment value covers 5,981 other boxes.

F03.determination: The USD 1,675,696 bunker value reconciles as USD 604,854.90 remaining plus USD 1,306,320.40 discharged and not reloaded, less USD 266,214.20 future voyage consumption, plus USD 30,734.90 made good.

F04.determination: Contract populations, rather than a preference for the newest rules, control: four named bill families use YAR 1974/1990 and six named bill families use YAR 1994.

F05.determination: The principal allowances are shared between the rule sets, but the adjustment separates the interest treatment before producing the population-weighted final claim.

F06.determination: The USD 385,513 casualty-repair amount is particular average, deducted from vessel sound value; it is not a refloating sacrifice allowance in the general-average fund.

F07.determination: No vessel sacrifice damage was found in the salvage operations, so no vessel sacrifice amount should be invented or moved into allowances.

F08.determination: The reported box damage did not damage its cargo and was limited; the adjusters expressly made no general-average allowance for it.

F09.determination: The salvage payment of USD 9,502,385.22, including bank charges against an all-in USD 9,500,000 settlement, is admitted general-average expenditure.

F10.determination: Quantum and enforceability must remain separate: the issued allocation remains the historical computation, but it does not establish a collectible debt against cargo after the operative fault decision.

F11.determination: The owners are not entitled to recover the respondent cargo interests' contribution because a causative breach of the carriage contract is actionable fault.

F12.determination: The missing danger warning made the pre-voyage passage plan and working chart defective, and that condition rendered the vessel unseaworthy.

F13.determination: The passage-plan defect was a real and effective cause of the master's decision to leave the buoyed fairway and of the grounding.

F14.determination: The due-diligence obligation is non-delegable for work needed to make the vessel seaworthy; competent crew, charts and systems did not discharge it when the entrusted planning work was performed without reasonable care.

F15.determination: The navigation-or-management exception cannot answer a causative breach of the prior seaworthiness duty, even though the relevant work involved navigational judgment.

F16.determination: The operative result is dismissal of the owners' appeal, preserving dismissal of their contribution claim against the respondent cargo interests.

F17.determination: Keep the payment populations separate: most cargo interests had paid, while about 8% resisted and the litigated demand against respondents was approximately USD 800,000, not the whole USD 9,826,980.60 cargo contribution shown in the adjustment.

F18.determination: The 8% cash-deposit call was provisional security and must not be used as the final debt or rate; the final blended adjustment rate is 2.67460000%.

F19.determination: The supplied records do not determine automatic refunds for cargo interests that already paid, or universal guarantee releases; account terms, settlements, parties, limitation and payment evidence are not shown and require separate review.

F20.determination: Operationally, stop collection of the dismissed respondent claim, retain the quantum schedule, and reconcile each cash deposit, bond or guarantee against its account and governing instrument before refund or release.

F21.determination: Section A is not wholly admitted merely because every item concerns salvage: gross USD 10,310,794.05 divides into USD 107,530.81 remainder and USD 10,203,263.24 general average.

F22.determination: Section B gross USD 1,158,590.22 divides into USD 16,679.20 remainder and USD 1,141,911.02 general average.

F23.determination: Section C gross USD 37,761.14 is carried wholly to general average with no remainder.

F24.determination: Section D gross USD 423,848.94 divides into USD 1,252.16 remainder and USD 422,596.78 general average.

F25.determination: The four sections close at gross USD 11,930,994.35, remainder USD 125,462.17 and admitted principal USD 11,805,532.18.

F26.determination: Voucher B5 must be split by timing: of gross USD 20,866.30, USD 13,910.87 is remainder and USD 6,955.43 enters general average; the post-refloating survey portion is particular average.

F27.determination: Voucher B9 of USD 2,768.33 for crew-change and visa agency expense is wholly remainder and contributes zero to general average.

F28.determination: Voucher D10b is not wholly admitted or wholly rejected: gross USD 4,327.10 divides into USD 1,252.16 remainder and USD 3,074.94 general average.

F29.determination: Rule XX commission is USD 226,130.84 at 2% on the printed USD 11,306,541.09 base, not on the gross or the whole admitted-principal total; the supplied record does not support manufacturing a different base. Recomputing 2% of the printed base rounds to 226130.82, 0.02 below the printed 226130.84; disclose the discrepancy while preserving the printed bridge pending clarification.

F30.determination: The interest columns remain separate: 7% Rule XXI interest is stated as USD 509,909.02 for YAR 1974/1990 and USD 711,848.06 for YAR 1994, producing pre-fee subtotals USD 12,541,572.04 and USD 12,743,511.08.

F31.determination: The detailed Rule XXI date-and-base calculation is said to be in the adjusters' file and is not supplied, so the two reported interest amounts can be reconciled but not independently re-performed.

F32.determination: Common adjustment fees and expenses of USD 865,990.66 are added to both pre-fee subtotals, closing the rule funds at USD 13,407,562.70 and USD 13,609,501.74.

F33.determination: The adjusters' statement that payment evidence was seen or confirmed concerns the disbursement accounts examined for the adjustment, except their fees; it is not evidence that every cargo contribution was paid.

F34.determination: Security collection status is not contribution-payment status: the record describes about 95% of consignments secured by late July and later all but some low-value consolidated shipments secured, without an account-level cash-payment conclusion.

F35.determination: The 8% deposit call and the approximately 8% resisting cargo population are different measures; neither the approximately USD 800,000 litigated claim nor the USD 9,826,980.60 aggregate cargo contribution can be substituted for the other.

F36.determination: The adjustment says standard Average Bonds and Guarantees incorporated a Non-Separation-Agreement, but it does not supply an account-level instrument register or terms supporting a blanket release or demand.

F37.determination: The adjustment records administration of a dedicated trust account for cash deposits, but supplies no current balance, beneficial entitlement, allocation, release, or refund ledger.

F38.determination: Security-collection expenses and adjustment administration remain part of the issued historical allowance ledger; the judgment does not direct their reclassification or a new adjustment.

F39.determination: The approximately USD 800,000 respondent claim and approximately 8% population are procedural aggregates, not an identified account schedule; respondent membership and exact per-account amounts remain unshown.

F40.determination: Dismissal of the owners' appeal resolves the litigated recovery claim but the supplied judgment contains no account-level monetary, refund, or security-release order for other interests.

F41.determination: The owners' uncharted-shoal account was a party position, not a finding. The trial court instead found that the defective passage plan and omitted warning caused the master's unsafe departure from the fairway and the grounding.

F42.determination: The conventional burden allocation remained operative: cargo had to establish causative unseaworthiness, then the owners had to establish due diligence. Cargo's proposed Volcafe reversal was rejected at trial and not pursued on appeal.

F43.determination: The trial court did not find that the relevant Notice to Mariners was absent from the vessel and found the separate sounding corrections were already marked; those allegations added no causative fault or unseaworthiness.

F44.determination: The absence of official electronic charts was not unseaworthiness in 2011 because no such SOLAS carriage requirement then applied and coverage was limited; any exclusive reliance on the installed display was left as negligent navigation, not an accepted additional seaworthiness defect.

F45.determination: The trial court rejected the collateral bridge-team and incompetence theories: no disabling lack of bridge communication was inferred and the experienced master was not found incompetent.

F46.determination: The master may have been tired, but fatigue was not shown materially to impair his decisions; on the balance of probabilities the defective passage plan caused the unsafe decision.

F47.determination: A contractual-deviation theory was unnecessary to decide and was rejected in any event: the short departure from the fairway was negligent navigation, not a radical change of voyage.

F48.determination: The intermediate appeal proceeded on the trial factual platform, which was not challenged. Two owner appeal grounds received permission, while a late third ground was abandoned and was not decided.

F49.determination: Of the cargo respondents' alternative grounds, the defective-working-chart route supported affirmance, but the alleged absence of a proper passage-planning system or culture was rejected; the latter is not an additional finding against the owners.

F50.determination: The procedural chain has one continuing recovery consequence: the first-instance dismissal of the owners' contribution claim was left in place when both the intermediate and final appeals were dismissed; the successive decisions are not separate payment or refund events.
F50.evidence: first_instance_judgment.pdf para.129; court_of_appeal_judgment.pdf para.76; final_judgment.pdf paras.30, 33, 146

F51.determination: The separate sounding corrections were already marked on the working chart when recorded after the casualty; the trial court did not infer a late addition and found no unseaworthiness on that ground.

F52.determination: The experienced master was not found incompetent; the trial court rejected cargo's requested inference from his negligent acts.

F53.determination: If the master placed exclusive reliance on the electronic display, that was negligent navigation; it did not convert the rejected electronic-chart carriage allegation into an additional seaworthiness finding.

F54.determination: A late third owner ground at the intermediate appeal was abandoned and received no decision.

F55.determination: Cargo's proposed Volcafe burden-of-proof challenge was not pursued at the intermediate appeal.

F56.determination: The intermediate court rejected cargo's alternative contention that the trial judgment established a separate failure of passage-planning system or culture.

F57.determination: The two owner grounds for which permission was granted both failed, producing dismissal of the intermediate appeal.

F58.determination: The approximately USD 800,000 litigated demand is an aggregate for the resisting respondent population, not the USD 9,826,980.60 cargo contribution in the historical allocation.
F58.evidence: first_instance_judgment.pdf para.1; final_judgment.pdf para.20; general_average_adjustment.pdf p.95

F59.determination: The decision record does not support blanket release of bonds or guarantees for other cargo interests; each instrument and account status remains to be established.

F60.determination: The issued adjustment and schedule should be retained as the historical quantum baseline despite the respondent collection bar.

F61.determination: Each cash deposit, bond and guarantee requires account-by-account reconciliation to its governing instrument before any refund, release or demand.

F62.determination: Vessel interests lodged salvage security on behalf of cargo so the laden voyage could continue without separate cargo salvage security; that fact does not prove cargo paid its later general-average contribution.

F63.determination: Container interests supplied direct salvage security, a state separate from their general-average contribution and from the cargo security population.

F64.determination: The common-safety timeline did not end every allowance at refloating: after refloating on 26 May the vessel remained at a safe anchorage for about two days while discharged bunkers were reloaded, then resumed the voyage on 28 May.

F65.determination: The adjustment maps salvage to Rule VI, lightening and reshipping to Rule VIII, refuge and detention during bunker reloading to Rule XI, and other direct-consequence expenditure to Rule C or, for YAR 1994, Rule XI(d).

F66.determination: Pollution measures began as a consequence of the accident but remained conditional for every refloating attempt because the hull condition was unknown; on that basis the adjuster admitted the entire period rather than excluding it as ordinary pollution response.

F67.determination: The same pollution-prevention expenditure is routed differently by contract population: Rule XI(d) under YAR 1994, but Rules C and VI under YAR 1974/1990.

F68.determination: Voucher B12 pollution-prevention expenditure of USD 264,705.06 is carried wholly to general average, with no remainder, consistently with the adjuster's causal note.

F69.determination: Voucher B6, USD 3,019.42 for reloading containers on the substitute vessel after refloating, is wholly admitted against reloading cost saved on the original vessel; the post-refloating date alone does not exclude it.

F70.determination: Voucher B5 applies the opposite post-refloating treatment: gross USD 20,866.30 splits into USD 13,910.87 remainder and USD 6,955.43 admitted because the later underwater survey belongs to the vessel's particular-average claim.

F71.determination: Voucher B9 crew-change and visa agency expense of USD 2,768.33 is wholly excluded even though it appears within the China expenditure sequence.

F72.determination: The D10 travel heading does not control every sub-trip: May 2011, July 2013 and February 2014 travel is wholly admitted, while June 2012 voucher D10b is split from gross USD 4,327.10 into USD 1,252.16 remainder and USD 3,074.94 admitted.

F73.determination: A6a Marseille-meeting travel is itself split: gross USD 15,035.72 divides into USD 5,011.91 remainder and USD 10,023.81 general average.

F74.determination: The A6 subitems do not share one treatment: London meetings of USD 3,294.59 and the February 2014 China meeting of USD 5,647.62 are admitted, while the China survey of USD 6,521.27 is wholly remainder.

F75.determination: A6 miscellaneous time and expense of USD 24,000 is divided into USD 12,000 remainder and USD 12,000 general average, whereas the USD 51,000 salvage bail fee is wholly admitted.

F76.determination: Section C is wholly admitted at USD 37,761.14 despite covering the post-refloating detention period: it combines two days of crew wages and maintenance with bunker and lube-oil consumption during refloating and detention while reloading bunkers.

F77.determination: Payment and loss classification remain separate: vessel interests paid the salvage settlement that is allowed in general average, while hull underwriters reportedly settled the vessel's particular-average claim and permanent casualty repairs reduce vessel contributory value.

F78.determination: The USD 173,591.67 premium for cargo salvage security is wholly admitted in the allowance ledger, but it remains a security cost rather than proof that the secured cargo interests paid their general-average contributions.

F79.determination: The bunker value bridge includes fuel discharged but not reloaded, deducts voyage consumption that would have occurred, and adds the bunker amount made good; physical absence at the end of the voyage does not by itself remove that interest from contribution.
